explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Josiah appoints the priests to their duties and encourages them in the service of the house of the LORD. He doesn't just hand over the job list, he adds a little push of confidence with it. Those are the bosses people remember, because a schedule with a kind word on top goes down a lot easier.

Tests sounds like a surprise inspection, but the verse never says that. Josiah appoints the priests to their duties and encourages them. I'd take a pep talk over an inspection any day of the week. The word in the text is encourages.

Warns is a fair guess for a king with a giant job list, but the verse sounds warmer than that. Josiah appoints the priests to their duties and encourages them. Nobody's getting a finger wagged at them here. I think a priest hearing that walks into the work standing a little taller.

Close, but it's the opposite. Josiah tells the Levites to put the holy ark in the temple built by Solomon, David's son and a king of Israel. Then he says, “It is not to be carried around on your shoulders.” So the ark gets a place to stay, and the shoulders get a break.

That's right, it's False. Josiah tells the Levites to put the holy ark in the temple built by Solomon, David's son and a king of Israel. Then he says, “It is not to be carried around on your shoulders.” I bet some Levite shoulders were relieved to hear it.

That's right, baker. Josiah tells the Levites to make preparations for their fellow countrymen. The Levites aren't only getting ready for themselves. Josiah also tells them, "Now serve the LORD your God and His people Israel." (2 Chronicles 35:3)

Nice try, but there are no envoys from Babylon anywhere in this passage. Josiah tells the Levites to make preparations for their fellow countrymen. These are the people of his own land. Nobody's rolling out a welcome mat for a foreign delegation here.

The Gibeonites don't show up in this passage at all. Josiah tells the Levites to slaughter the Passover lambs, consecrate themselves, and make preparations for their fellow countrymen. That's the group the verse names. Sometimes the answer is the plain one sitting right in the sentence.

Yes, baker. Josiah tells the Levites to prepare so they can carry out “…the word of the LORD given by Moses.” Moses was Israel's leader, and Josiah points them to what he gave. So this whole service rests on something already given, not on a new idea from the king.

This one's actually True. Josiah tells the Levites to make preparations “…to carry out the word of the LORD given by Moses.” Moses was Israel's leader, and Josiah points straight to the word the LORD gave through him. It's right there in verse 6, so no shame in missing it.

You got it, baker. The verse says Josiah contributed the lambs, goats and bulls from his own flocks and herds. That's thirty-three thousand animals coming out of the king's own pocket. When the boss pays for the party himself, you know he means it.

explanations.answer: A new tax on the people
explanations.explanation: No new tax appears anywhere in this passage. The verse says Josiah gave the 30,000 lambs and goats plus the 3,000 bulls from his own flocks and herds. His officials contribute too, in the verses that follow.

The temple treasury doesn't come up in this passage. The text says Josiah contributed the animals from his own flocks and herds. That means the animals were his, not borrowed from some storehouse. A king reaching into his own pocket speaks louder than any budget meeting.

That's it, baker. The verse says Josiah's officials also contributed willingly to the people, priests and Levites. Nobody had to drag them to the giving table. Willingly is the word the text uses, and it's the right one.

Grudgingly would be a sour way to give, but that's not what the verse says. Josiah's officials contributed willingly to the people, priests and Levites. The text gives that word, willingly, and nothing sour.

Secret isn't the word the verse uses. It says the officials contributed willingly to the people, priests and Levites. The next verses name Hilkiah, Zechariah and Jehiel, the chief officials of the house of God. They also name Conaniah, an officer of the Levites, along with his brothers.

The jobs are flipped in that one. The verse says the priests splattered the blood handed to them, and the Levites skinned the animals. So the blood goes to the priests and the skinning goes to the Levites.
You got it, it's False. The verse says the priests splattered the blood handed to them, and the Levites skinned the animals. So it's blood for the priests and skinning for the Levites.

That's right, baker. The verse says they roasted the Passover animals on the fire according to the regulation. The other holy offerings were boiled in pots, kettles and bowls. So the Passover animals are the ones that got the fire.

An oven is my kind of answer, but the text says something else. They roasted the Passover animals on the fire according to the regulation. No clay ovens are mentioned. The cooking here is done over fire.
Drying in the sun doesn't appear in the verse. It says they roasted the Passover animals on the fire according to the regulation. So the heat here comes from the fire, not the sun.
Yes, baker. The verse says they boiled the other holy offerings in pots, kettles and bowls and quickly brought them to all the people. Notice the word quickly. It's right there in verse 13.

This one's actually True. The verse says they boiled the other holy offerings in pots, kettles and bowls and quickly brought them to all the people. The word quickly is right there in verse 13. When the food's hot and the people are waiting, speed matters.

That's right, baker. The priests were offering burnt offerings and fat until nightfall, so the Levites made preparations for themselves and for the priests. The Levites handled the prep so the priests could keep working. Until nightfall! I get worn out after one double batch, so I respect that.

Temple servants don't appear in this passage. The verse says the Levites made preparations for themselves and for the priests. The priests were busy with burnt offerings and fat until nightfall. So the Levites stepped in.

The Rechabites aren't mentioned anywhere in this passage. The text says the Levites made preparations for themselves and for the priests. The priests were tied up with burnt offerings and fat until nightfall. The Levites covered the prep.

You got it, baker. The singers, the descendants of Asaph, were at their stations according to the command of David, king of Israel. The verse also names Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun the king's seer. Josiah is following a plan that was set up long before him.

Hezekiah isn't named anywhere in this passage. The verse says the singers were at their stations according to the command of David, king of Israel, along with Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun the king's seer. David is the king this verse points to. Josiah is following the older plan.

Jehoshaphat doesn't show up in this passage. The singers were at their stations according to the command of David, king of Israel. The verse names Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun the king's seer alongside him. So David's the king to pick.

That's right, baker. The verse says the Israelites who were present observed the Passover at that time, as well as the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days. That's a whole week of celebrating. It's a lot longer than one afternoon.

Three days would be a good stretch, but the verse says more. The Israelites who were present observed the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days. That's a full week, not a long weekend. It's all there in verse 17.

Forty days is a big number, but it isn't the one in this verse. The Israelites who were present observed the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days. That's one week. Forty days of celebrating and my ovens would file a complaint.

You got it, baker. The verse says, “No such Passover had been observed in Israel since the days of Samuel the prophet.” It also says none of the kings of Israel ever observed a Passover like the one Josiah observed. That's a long stretch of time with nothing like it.

Elijah is a fine guess, but he isn't the name in the verse. It says, “No such Passover had been observed in Israel since the days of Samuel the prophet.” Samuel is the one the text points back to. It's a big, big look back.

Elisha is a fine guess, but he isn't the name in the verse. It says, “No such Passover had been observed in Israel since the days of Samuel the prophet.” None of the kings of Israel observed one like Josiah's, either. That's how rare this Passover was.
